  - text: S1
  - heading "Summary" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Executive overview of what this item covers, key takeaways, and how its timeline and scope affect freight operations.
  - paragraph: "An operations profile of India's road freight and port sector from an ICCT policy commentary (September 15, 2025) and a WRI India programme page: freight cost weight, the electric truck scheme, draft fuel-efficiency rules and port targets."
  - paragraph: Why it matters
  - paragraph: India's logistics costs are about 13% of GDP nationally and 70% of freight moves by road; the pages do not tie either figure to a lane cost. Only 869 electric medium- and heavy-duty freight vehicles run against 6.3 million trucks, held back by upfront cost and limited charging, so an electric truck option on Indian lanes is a supply question first. Draft fuel-efficiency rules and port targets for 2030 and 2047 may change which trucks carriers can buy and how ports are powered. The pages state no tariff, fuel price or haulage rate.
  - paragraph: What it changes
  - paragraph: India has 869 electric freight vehicles against 6.3 million trucks, so an electric truck option needs carrier confirmation; draft fuel rules and port targets are still ahead.
  - paragraph: Key data
  - paragraph: "Road freight: 70% of India's freight moves by road; medium/heavy trucks are 44% of transport GHG share on just 3% of vehicles"
  - paragraph: "Logistics costs: about 13% of GDP nationally; 10-15% of company expenses at the corporate level"
  - paragraph: Fewer than 900 electric medium- and heavy-duty freight vehicles in service nationally
  - paragraph: "Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047: port capacity from 2500 to over 10000 MMTPA; shore power at all major ports by 2047"

  - heading "Substantive findings" [level=2]
  - button "Collapse ▴" [expanded]
  - paragraph: Detailed analytical breakdown of operational drivers, cost baselines, mode impacts, and strategic talking points.
  - paragraph: Operational cost baseline
  - paragraph: This profile covers India's road freight and port sector, drawn from a policy commentary by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), dated September 15, 2025, and a programme page of WRI India, a research institute. The pages state no industrial electricity tariff, diesel price per litre, driver or warehouse labour rate, port handling charge or haulage rate, so a unit cost baseline cannot be given and none is invented.
  - paragraph: Feasibility of operational choices
  - paragraph:
    - text: "Electric trucks: «India has only 869 electric medium- and heavy-duty freight vehicles», against the fleet of 6.3 million trucks quoted in section 1. WRI India gives the reason: «The high upfront cost of electric trucks, coupled with limited charging infrastructure, remains a significant roadblock.» It adds that «Additional barriers, including a fragmented industry, the absence of standardized contracts, and a lack of strong regulatory mandates, further slow progress.» Direction exists on the policy side: «In July 2025, the Ministry of Heavy Industries released guidelines for electric trucks under the PM e-DRIVE scheme», and the e-FAST India platform, on which WRI India is lead partner, reports «securing commitments for 7,750 e-trucks at the Clean Energy Ministerial.», with «Facilitating early e-truck pilots in Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra»."
    - emphasis: "Analytical inference:"
    - text: resting on these sentences, the position is restricted by cost and charging rather than barred by any rule the pages state, and the 7,750 trucks committed are many times the 869 on the road, so the first constraint on an electric truck option for a forwarder's Indian lanes is availability and charging, and the pages give no price or range for a truck to cost it.

  - paragraph: "Truck makers must cut average emissions: targets in Europe and California, battery prices, chargers and the haulier's cost"
  - text: Written for an earlier membership of this theme; the items below are today's.
  - paragraph: What it means
  - paragraph: "For a freight operator with no sustainability background: these rules do not order a haulier to buy an electric truck. They order the maker to lower the average emissions of the trucks it sells. In Europe, the Regulation applies to new heavy-duty vehicles of categories N2 and N3, that is, new heavy trucks. Article 3a(1): reductions are measured against the average CO2 emissions of the reporting period of the year 2019. A maker that misses pays per unit of excess: from 2025 to 2029 the premium is excess emissions times 4 250 EUR/gCO2/tkm, and from 2030 onwards the premium is excess emissions times 6 800 EUR/gCO2/tkm."
  - paragraph: "Battery prices have fallen: Battery pack prices for lithium-ion fell 20% in 2024 — the largest single-year drop since 2017 — and a further 8% reduction has been reported for 2025 by BloombergNEF via CALSTART, putting the current market price at approximately $108/kWh. The obstacles that remain are named in interviews reported by a clean-transport research council: ICCT interviews: barriers are lack of publicly accessible charging and refueling for trucks, limited truck availability, limited range and higher purchase costs."
  - paragraph:
    - emphasis: "Analytical inference:"
    - text: the European law itself expects makers to meet the later targets by selling more zero-emission trucks (see Watch); whether hauliers buy them then turns on the purchase cost and the charging these records describe.
  - paragraph:
    - emphasis: "Analytical inference:"
    - text: the cost reaches a forwarder through its road subcontractors' truck purchase and charging costs; no record here gives a per-kilometre cost of an electric truck against a diesel one, so the size of that change is not shown.
  - paragraph: What follows on Operations
  - paragraph: "In the United States, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles produce about 26 percent of transportation emissions, and Over 94% of transportation fuel is petroleum-based. Charging is a constraint: one source counts 384 open federally funded chargers nationally as of April 2025. These are public points funded by two programs that support public electric vehicle charging infrastructure, and the source says the count does not support calling the network ready for commercial freight at scale. Later, a federal judge issued a final judgment on January 30, 2026 in Washington v. U.S. Department of Transportation, determining USDOT's February-to-August pause of the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program to be a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act; no record here shows its effect on the chargers opened."
  - paragraph: What to watch
  - list:
    - listitem: "Europe's charging infrastructure law is reviewed: By 31 December 2026 and every five years thereafter, the Commission shall review this Regulation. A clean-trucking advocacy alliance has set out its asks: ECTA published its priorities for the review of the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation as a position paper on 28 May 2026. A revised law would appear on Regulations."
    - listitem: "The Commission must report on fleet initiatives: by 30 June 2027 the Commission shall submit a report on initiatives to increase the share of zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles owned or leased by large fleet operators. If it proposes duties on fleets, a forwarder that runs or contracts large fleets would see them on Regulations."
    - listitem: "The European truck emission law's own review: By 31 December 2027 the Commission shall review the effectiveness and impact of the Regulation, in particular as regards climate neutrality at the latest by 2050. Its result would appear on Regulations."
    - listitem: The next vehicle pollutant standard reaches new models of buses, coaches, heavy trucks and heavy trailers (It shall apply from 29 May 2028 for new types of vehicles), and a year later every new vehicle of those kinds.
    - listitem: "The next step for makers: 45 % for all vehicle sub-groups other than vocational vehicles for the reporting periods of the years 2030 to 2034. The law's recital says that with these targets manufacturers are to deploy significantly more zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles on the Union market."
    - listitem: "In California a maker covers its obligations with credits earned from zero-emission sales; ZEV or NZEV credits generated in the 2021, 2022 and 2023 model years expire at of the end of the 2030 model year, and are no longer available to be used to meet compliance for 2031 and later model years. The next link this theme needs is on Market Intel: a published total cost per kilometre for electric against diesel heavy trucks in a European country or in California."
